items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis: +4.0 μC at x = 0.00 m and -2.0 μC at x = 0.30 m. What is the net electric field at the point x = 0.20 m? Give magnitude and direction. (Use k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2; carry units through.)

items.answer:
(a) Outside (r > R): The field is radially outward and has magnitude E = (1/(4πε0))·Q / r^2 (units N C^-1). The shell behaves like a point charge at its centre because of spherical symmetry (Gauss's law).

(b) On the surface (r = R): The field is radially outward with magnitude E = (1/(4πε0))·Q / R^2 (N C^-1); this is the value from the outside expression evaluated at r = R.

(c) Inside (r < R): The field is zero (E = 0 N C^-1) everywhere inside the hollow shell. By spherical symmetry and Gauss's law, any Gaussian surface inside encloses no net charge, so the net flux and therefore the field must be zero.

rubric.criteria: Correct description of the electric field in the three regions (outside, on surface, inside) with appropriate dependence on r and brief justification.

items.stem: A thin insulating spherical shell of radius R carries a total charge +Q uniformly distributed over its surface. In words (no calculus), describe the electric field E (magnitude, direction, and dependence on distance r) for each region: (a) outside the shell (r > R), (b) on the surface (r = R), and (c) inside the shell (r < R). Briefly state the reason for each behaviour.

items.answer: A conductor is a material in which valence electrons (or charge carriers) can move freely through the material; an insulator is a material in which electrons are tightly bound to atoms and cannot move freely. When a solid conducting sphere receives extra electrons, the electrons move freely and redistribute themselves over the outer surface of the sphere until electrostatic equilibrium is reached; there is no excess charge left in the interior and the electric field inside the conductor is zero. By contrast, when a solid insulating rod receives extra electrons (for example by rubbing), the extra electrons stay localized near the region where they were placed and do not move freely to the whole surface; the charge remains stuck in that part of the insulator. An everyday example of a conductor is copper (used for electrical wiring because it allows current to flow easily). An everyday example of an insulator is plastic (used to coat wires and make handles because it prevents charge flow).

rubric.criteria: Accuracy and completeness of definitions, description of charge distribution in conductor and insulator, and provision of correct everyday examples.

levels.descriptor: Provides correct definitions for conductor and insulator (electron mobility stated); correctly describes that excess charge on a conducting sphere moves to the outer surface (interior field zero) and that excess charge on an insulating rod remains localized where placed; gives one correct everyday example of a conductor with use and one correct everyday example of an insulator with use.
levels.label: Full credit

items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis in vacuum. Charge Q1 = +3.0 μC is at x = 0.00 m and charge Q2 = −1.0 μC is at x = 0.20 m. Calculate the electric field vector (magnitude and direction) at the point P located at x = 0.10 m. Give your answer in N C^−1 and state the direction along the x-axis.
items.working:
Constants and conversions:
Permittivity ε0 = 8.85 × 10^−12 C^2 N^−1 m^−2; k = 1/(4π ε0) = 8.99 × 10^9 N m^2 C^−2.
Convert charges: Q1 = +3.0 μC = 3.0 × 10^−6 C; Q2 = −1.0 μC = −1.0 × 10^−6 C.
Positions: x1 = 0.00 m, xP = 0.10 m, x2 = 0.20 m.
Distance from Q1 to P: r1 = xP − x1 = 0.10 m (field due to Q1 at P points away from +Q1, i.e. to the right, +x).
Magnitude E1 = k |Q1| / r1^2 = (8.99 × 10^9)(3.0 × 10^−6) / (0.10)^2
E1 = (8.99 × 10^9 × 3.0 × 10^−6) / 0.01
E1 = (26.97 × 10^3) / 0.01 = 2.697 × 10^6 N C^−1 → 2.70 × 10^6 N C^−1 to three significant figures, direction +x.
Distance from Q2 to P: r2 = x2 − xP = 0.20 − 0.10 = 0.10 m (field due to Q2 at P: Q2 is negative so field points toward Q2, i.e. to the right as well, +x).
Magnitude E2 = k |Q2| / r2^2 = (8.99 × 10^9)(1.0 × 10^−6) / (0.10)^2
E2 = (8.99 × 10^3) / 0.01 = 8.99 × 10^5 N C^−1 → 8.99 × 10^5 N C^−1.
Both fields point in the +x direction, so add magnitudes:
Enet = E1 + E2 = 2.697 × 10^6 + 8.99 × 10^5 = (2.697 + 0.899) × 10^6 = 3.596 × 10^6 N C^−1.
Round to two significant figures appropriate to input: 3.60 × 10^6 N C^−1 to the right.
(If using three significant figures consistent with the charges: 3.60 × 10^6 N C^−1 to the +x direction.)
Note: Depending on rounding conventions, an answer of about 3.6 × 10^6 N C^−1, +x, earns full credit.

items.answer: Option 1: +Q is the source that produces the electric field and +q is the small test charge that experiences force F = qE; +q must be small or fixed so it does not disturb +Q, ensuring the measured field is that of +Q alone.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct. The source charge +Q creates the field; the test charge +q probes it by feeling a force F = qE. To define the field of +Q, +q must be small or fixed so it does not significantly alter +Q or the field configuration.
options.text: +Q is the source charge that produces the electric field; +q is the test charge that experiences the force. +q must be small (or fixed so it does not disturb +Q) so the field being measured is that of +Q alone.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Wrong: this implies the test charge and source are interchangeable and that the field is dominated by +q because of proximity. The test charge should be negligible so it does not produce a comparable field; the measured field is that due to +Q, not +q.
options.text: Both +Q and +q are equally source charges that produce separate electric fields; the measured field at a point is just the field of +q at that point because it is closer.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Wrong: a test charge need not be zero; it must be small enough that its own field is negligible. Taking q -> 0 is a limiting concept for defining E = F/q, but physically we use a small nonzero q that does not disturb the source.
options.text: A test charge must be exactly zero to avoid changing the field; therefore +q should be taken to zero for the electric field of +Q to exist.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Wrong: the electric field is a property of the source charge(s) and space, not of the test charge. The test charge experiences the field (force F = qE); it does not 'have' the field being measured.
options.text: The electric field is a property of the test charge +q and is measured by observing how +Q moves in response to +q.

items.stem: A fixed charge +Q sits at the origin and creates an electric field. A small positive test charge +q is brought close to +Q to measure the field. Which statement correctly describes the roles of +Q and +q when defining the electric field of +Q?

items.answer:
Sketch: Field lines start at the positive charge (+q) and end at the negative charge (−q); lines are more curved near the space between the charges and symmetric in a dipole shape. Arrows point away from +q and toward −q.

Three properties (one per letter):
(a) Direction: The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the electric field there, so arrows point away from the positive charge and toward the negative charge.
(b) Spacing (density): The local density of field lines represents the relative magnitude of the electric field; where lines are closer together the field is stronger, and where they are farther apart the field is weaker.
(c) Number of lines: The absolute number of lines drawn is not a unique physical property — one may draw more or fewer lines to illustrate strength; only the relative density and direction have physical meaning.

rubric.criteria: Correct sketch and three accurate statements about (a) direction, (b) density representing field strength, and (c) non-uniqueness of absolute line count.

levels.descriptor: Sketch shows lines beginning at +q and ending at −q with arrows pointing away from +q toward −q (dipole-like shape). Statement (a) correctly says tangent gives field direction and arrows point away from +q/toward −q. Statement (b) correctly says local line density indicates relative field strength (closer lines = stronger field). Statement (c) correctly says the absolute number of drawn lines is not an intrinsic physical property and may be chosen for illustration.

levels.descriptor: Sketch is mostly correct (lines generally from +q to −q) and two of the three statements are correct. For example, (a) and (b) correct but (c) missing or incorrect, or (a) correct while (b) and (c) provide partly correct ideas (e.g. mention density but not its meaning).
levels.label: 2 marks

levels.descriptor: Sketch is incorrect (e.g. arrows pointing toward +q or lines crossing) or fewer than two of the three required statements are correct. Statements that assert the absolute number of lines is a fixed physical quantity or confuse direction/density are scored zero.

(4 marks)

Shows understanding that field ~1/r^3. (2 marks)

items.stem: Two point charges +q and −q are placed on the x-axis at x = +a and x = −a respectively. Find an expression for the electric field magnitude E on the +x-axis at a point x = r where r >> a. Using a binomial expansion to first order in a/r, show that the field falls off as 1/r^3 and express your result in terms of the dipole moment p = q(2a). State the direction of the field. (4 marks)
items.working:
1. Exact fields from each charge at point x = r (r > a):
   E+ from +q at x = +a points in +x direction with magnitude E+ = (1/4πε0) q / (r − a)^2.
   E− from −q at x = −a points in +x direction (since −q attracts a positive test charge toward −x, but located at −a gives field at r directed toward −a, i.e. −x; however because the charge is negative the field at r is toward −a which is in the −x direction; careful: using signs explicitly below gives correct net direction).
2. Use algebra with signed fields (taking +x direction positive):
   Field from +q: E+ = (1/4πε0) q / (r − a)^2 (positive).
   Field from −q: distance to −q is r + a, and field points toward −q, i.e. in the −x direction, so E− = −(1/4πε0) q / (r + a)^2.
   Net field: E = E+ + E− = (1/4πε0) q [1/(r − a)^2 − 1/(r + a)^2].
3. Combine the difference of squares:
   1/(r − a)^2 − 1/(r + a)^2 = [(r + a)^2 − (r − a)^2] / [(r − a)^2 (r + a)^2]
   Numerator: (r^2 + 2ar + a^2) − (r^2 − 2ar + a^2) = 4ar.
   So the difference = 4ar / [(r − a)^2 (r + a)^2].
   Thus E = (1/4πε0) q (4ar) / [(r − a)^2 (r + a)^2].
4. For r >> a, approximate (r ± a)^2 ≈ r^2(1 ± a/r)^2 ≈ r^2(1 ± 2a/r) to first order, but product (r − a)^2(r + a)^2 ≈ (r^2 − a^2)^2 ≈ r^4 (1 − a^2/r^2)^2 ≈ r^4 to leading order. Therefore to leading order
   E ≈ (1/4πε0) q (4ar) / r^4 = (1/4πε0) (4qa) / r^3.
5. Write in terms of the dipole moment p = q(2a): then 4qa = 2p, so
   E ≈ (1/4πε0) (2p) / r^3.
6. Direction: the sign of E found above is positive, so the field is along +x (away from the dipole on the positive axis). Units are N C−1, showing the field scales as 1/r^3.

(End of working.)

items.answer: Φ = (E · n̂) dS, where n̂ is the unit normal to the area. Reason: the vector area element is dS = n̂ dS, so flux is E · dS = (E · n̂) dS (units: (N/C)·m² = N·m²/C), which picks the component of E perpendicular to the surface.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Incorrect: If θ is the angle between E and the surface plane, then cosθ equals the component of E parallel to the plane, not the component through the normal. This confuses the angle reference; the correct through-surface component uses the angle to the normal.
options.text: Φ = E dS cosθ, where θ is the angle between E and the surface plane

options.label: B
options.rationale: Correct: By definition the vector area element is dS = n̂ dS, so the flux through the element is E · dS = (E · n̂) dS. Units: E (N/C) × area (m²) gives N·m²/C, and the dot product takes the component of E normal to the surface.
options.text: Φ = (E · n̂) dS, where n̂ is the unit normal to the area

options.label: C
options.rationale: Incorrect: The cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both E and the area vector and does not measure the scalar flux through the surface. This mistakes perpendicular-area magnitude for the scalar dot-product flux.
options.text: Φ = E × dS, the cross product of the electric field and the area element

options.label: D
options.rationale: Incorrect: Φ = E dS sinθ uses the sine of the angle to the normal, which gives the component of E perpendicular to the normal (i.e., parallel to the surface). This confuses sine and cosine for the normal component.
options.text: Φ = E dS sinθ, where θ is the angle between E and the unit normal n̂

items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis: q1 = +3.0 µC at x = 0.00 m and q2 = −2.0 µC at x = +0.50 m. Using Coulomb's law, calculate (a) the magnitude of the electrostatic force on q1 due to q2 and (b) the direction of that force. Give the force as a magnitude with units and state its direction along the x-axis.
items.working:
Step 1 — write Coulomb's law (magnitude): F = k |q1 q2| / r^2, where k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2·C^−2.
Step 2 — substitute values with units: q1 = 3.0×10^−6 C, q2 = −2.0×10^−6 C (use absolute value for magnitude), r = 0.50 m.
F = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2·C^−2) × (3.0×10^−6 C) × (2.0×10^−6 C) / (0.50 m)^2.
Step 3 — compute numerator: (8.99×10^9) × (6.0×10^−12 C^2) = 8.99×6.0×10^(9−12) N·m^2 = 53.94×10^(−3) N·m^2 = 0.05394 N·m^2.
Step 4 — compute denominator: (0.50 m)^2 = 0.25 m^2.
Step 5 — divide: F = 0.05394 N·m^2 / 0.25 m^2 = 0.21576 N ≈ 0.216 N.
Step 6 — direction: q1 is positive and q2 is negative → attraction. q2 is at +0.50 m relative to q1 at 0.00 m, so the force on q1 is toward +x.
Final answer: F = 0.216 N, directed +x (toward q2).

So the electric field vector is

rubric.criteria: Correct setup and evaluation of the integral for the x-component of E; correct final expression and direction.

items.stem: A thin straight rod of length L lies on the x-axis from x = 0 to x = L and carries a uniform positive linear charge density λ (C m–1). Find the electric field vector E at point P on the x-axis located at x = −a (a > 0). Give the magnitude and direction of E in terms of λ, L, a and the constant k = 1/(4πϵ0).
items.working:
Take an element of length dx at position x (0 ≤ x ≤ L) carrying charge dq = λ dx (units C). The position of P is x_P = −a. The separation from dq to P is r = x − (−a) = x + a (units m). The contribution to the electric field at P from dq, using Coulomb's law, is dE = k dq / r^2, directed from dq toward P (for positive λ the field points from the positive charge toward P, i.e. in the +x direction because dq is to the right of P). The field contributions are all along the x-axis, so vector signs reduce to a sign for the x-component. Using +x as the direction from P toward the rod, dE_x = k (λ dx)/(x + a)^2.
Integrate over the rod from x = 0 to x = L:
E_x = ∫_{0}^{L} k λ (dx)/(x + a)^2.
Compute the integral: let u = x + a, du = dx, limits u = a to u = a + L.
E_x = k λ ∫_{u=a}^{a+L} u^{-2} du = k λ [−u^{-1}]_{a}^{a+L} = k λ (1/a − 1/(a + L)).
Units check: k (N m^2 C^{-2}) × λ (C m^{-1}) × (1/m) gives N C^{-1} = V m^{-1}, correct for electric field.
Therefore E = E_x ˆi = k λ (1/a − 1/(a + L)) ˆi, pointing in the +x direction for positive λ.

items.answer: Plane: choose a thin cylindrical pillbox with flat faces parallel to the plane so flux = 2 E A. Use Gauss's law 2 E A = (σ A)/ε0 ⇒ E = σ/(2 ε0) (units: C m^-2 / (C^2 N^-1 m^-2) = N C^-1). Wire: choose a coaxial cylinder of radius r and length L so flux = E (2π r L). Gauss: E(2π r L) = (λ L)/ε0 ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε0 r) (units: C m^-1 /(C^2 N^-1 m^-2 · m) = N C^-1). Shell: choose a spherical surface concentric with the shell. For r>R, E(4π r^2) = q/ε0 ⇒ E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) radial (units: C /(C^2 N^-1 m^-2 · m^2) = N C^-1). For r<R the enclosed charge is zero so E = 0.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct. For the infinite plane a pillbox gives flux through two faces: 2EA = Qenc/ε0 = σA/ε0 ⇒ E = σ/(2ε0). For the infinite wire a coaxial cylinder gives flux Φ = E(2πrL) = Qenc/ε0 = λL/ε0 ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε0 r). For the thin spherical shell a concentric sphere gives Φ = E(4πr^2) = q/ε0 for r>R ⇒ E = q/(4π ε0 r^2); if r<R no charge is enclosed so E = 0.
options.text: Plane: use a small cylindrical pillbox whose flat faces are parallel to the plane; E = σ/(2ε0) directed normal to the plane. Wire: use a coaxial cylindrical surface of radius r and length L; E = λ/(2π ε0 r) radially outward. Shell: use a spherical surface centered on the shell; for r>R, E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) radial, and for r<R, E = 0.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Wrong. The student chose a spherical Gaussian for the plane and got E = σ/ε0; this double-counts because the correct pillbox has two faces so each face sees σ/(2ε0). The wire answer has the wrong coefficient (λ/(π ε0 r)) from an incorrect flux area (using π instead of 2π). The sphere answers use wrong surfaces and wrong factors so enclosed-charge application is incorrect.
options.text: Plane: use a spherical Gaussian surface crossing the plane; E = σ/ε0 because both sides contribute. Wire: use a rectangular box around a short segment; E = λ/(π ε0 r) pointing outward. Shell: use a cylindrical surface coaxial with the shell; for r>R, E = q/(2π ε0 r^2) and inside E = q/(4π ε0 R^2).

options.label: C
options.rationale: Partially right for the plane and sphere outside, but wrong for the wire: E = λ/(4π ε0 r) is half the correct value. That error comes from using half the cylindrical surface area (e.g., using 2πrL where 4πrL was mistakenly assumed) or halving the flux; the correct cylinder gives 2πrL so E = λ/(2π ε0 r).
options.text: Plane: use a pillbox with faces parallel to the plane; E = σ/(2ε0) normal to the plane. Wire: use a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L; E = λ/(4π ε0 r) radial. Shell: use a spherical Gaussian surface centred on the shell; for r>R, E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) and for r<R, E = 0.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Plane and wire are mixed: the plane and wire formulas are partly correct in form but the shell-inside field is wrong. Saying E inside the shell equals q/(4π ε0 R^2) implies a nonzero field independent of r, which violates Gauss's law because a concentric sphere inside encloses zero charge so E must be zero.
options.text: Plane: use a pillbox with faces parallel to the plane; E = σ/(2ε0) normal to the plane. Wire: use a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L; E = λ/(2π ε0 r) radial. Shell: use a spherical Gaussian surface centred on the shell; for r>R, E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) and for r<R, E = q/(4π ε0 R^2).

items.answer: (a) The torque on the dipole is given by the vector cross product τ = p × E. Its magnitude is |τ| = pE sinθ, where θ is the angle between p and E. The torque tends to rotate the dipole so that p aligns with E. (b) (i) In a uniform electric field the net force on the dipole is zero because the forces on +q and −q are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, producing only a torque. (ii) In a non-uniform electric field the dipole can experience a net force because the field strength at the positions of +q and −q is different; the unequal forces do not cancel and produce a net translational force (which tends to pull the dipole toward regions of stronger field if aligned appropriately).

rubric.criteria: Correct expression and magnitude for torque; correct statements and brief explanations about net force in uniform and non-uniform fields.

levels.descriptor: States τ = p × E and |τ| = pE sinθ with θ defined; explains clearly that in a uniform field net force = 0 because forces on +q and −q cancel and that in a non-uniform field a net force can occur because the field differs at the two charges (unequal forces do not cancel).
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: Gives the correct torque formula (vector or magnitude) with θ, and correctly states that net force = 0 in a uniform field, but gives only a weak or incomplete explanation for the non-uniform case (e.g. says 'net force possible' without explaining unequal forces due to field gradient).

items.answer: Total initial charge = (+8.0 × 10^-19) + (−4.8 × 10^-19) = +3.2 × 10^-19 C. When touched, charge is conserved and shared equally, so final charge on each sphere = (3.2 × 10^-19 C) / 2 = +1.6 × 10^-19 C. Using q = n e with e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C gives n = q / e = (+1.6 × 10^-19 C) / (1.60 × 10^-19 C) = +1. Therefore each sphere has net charge +1.6 × 10^-19 C, corresponding to n = +1 (one elementary positive charge). A positive n means a deficit of one electron (one more proton's worth of positive charge than electrons); a negative n would mean an excess of electrons.

rubric.criteria: Correct final charge per sphere (C) and correct integer number of excess electrons n with clear use of q = n e and sign interpretation.

levels.descriptor: Correct total and final charge: Q_each = +1.6 × 10^-19 C, and correct calculation n = +1 with use of q = n e shown and a correct physical interpretation of positive n (deficit of one electron). Units carried correctly.
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: Final charge in coulombs correct (Q_each = +1.6 × 10^-19 C) but the conversion to n is missing, non-integer, or incorrectly signed OR the student gives n = 1 without showing use of q = n e. Units largely present.

levels.descriptor: Final charge incorrect and no correct use of q = n e, or arithmetic/misconception that charge is destroyed on contact (i.e. not conserved).
levels.label: No credit

items.stem: Two small conducting spheres A and B are isolated from the surroundings. Sphere A carries a net charge of +8.0 × 10^-19 C and sphere B carries a net charge of −4.8 × 10^-19 C. The two spheres are touched together and then separated. Using the charge quantisation relation q = n e with e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C, calculate (a) the final net charge on each sphere (in coulombs) and (b) the number n of excess electrons on each sphere after separation. State the sign of n and explain briefly what a positive or negative n means physically. (4 marks)
items.working:
Step 1: Compute total charge (conserve charge).
Q_total = Q_A + Q_B = +8.0 × 10^-19 C + (−4.8 × 10^-19 C) = +3.2 × 10^-19 C.
Step 2: Charge shared equally when conductors touch; each gets half.
Q_each = Q_total / 2 = (3.2 × 10^-19 C) / 2 = 1.6 × 10^-19 C.
Step 3: Convert to number of elementary charges using q = n e, e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C.
n = q / e = (1.6 × 10^-19 C) / (1.60 × 10^-19 C) = 1.0 → n = +1 (dimensionless).
Units carried: charges in coulombs throughout; e in coulombs so n is unitless.
Interpretation: n = +1 means each sphere is missing one electron compared with being neutral (a net positive elementary charge).

items.answer: Zero newtons per coulomb (0 N/C) at the midpoint. Work: distance from midpoint to each charge r = 0.10 m. Field from one charge E1 = k q / r^2 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(3.0×10^-6 C)/(0.10 m)^2 = 2.697×10^6 N/C. The other charge gives E2 = 2.697×10^6 N/C in the opposite direction, so vector sum E_net = E1 + E2 = 0 N/C.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct—each charge produces an electric field of magnitude E = kq/r^2 with r = 0.10 m: E = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(3.0×10^-6 C)/(0.10 m)^2 = 2.697×10^6 N/C. At the midpoint the two fields are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their vector sum is zero.
options.text: Zero newtons per coulomb (0 N/C) at the midpoint

options.label: B
options.rationale: This choice treats the field from one charge as the net field. The student forgot to add vector directions: both charges produce equal-magnitude fields at the midpoint but they point in opposite directions and cancel, so the net is not a single 2.7×10^6 N/C to the right.
options.text: 2.7 × 10^6 N/C pointing to the right (positive x)

options.label: C
options.rationale: This choice has the correct single-charge magnitude but the wrong direction for the net field. It mistakes the field from one charge for the net; because the two equal fields are opposite, they do not leave a net 2.7×10^6 N/C to the left.
options.text: 2.7 × 10^6 N/C pointing to the left (negative x)

options.label: D
options.rationale: This choice doubles the single-charge magnitude as if the two fields simply add in the same direction. The misconception is treating magnitudes as scalars to sum without accounting for direction; here the two equal fields are opposite and cancel, so you should not get 5.4×10^6 N/C.
options.text: 5.4 × 10^6 N/C pointing to the right (positive x)

rubric.criteria: Correct use of superposition to compute magnitudes of fields from each charge, correct vector sum and stated units/direction.

levels.descriptor: Correctly computes E1 and E2 with k and r^2 shown and units, adds them as vectors (noting both point +x), and gives final answer 3.60×10^6 N/C in the +x direction (or equivalent to three significant figures).
levels.label: Full marks

items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis in vacuum: charge q1 = +3.0 μC at x = 0.00 m and charge q2 = −1.0 μC at x = 0.20 m. Calculate the electric field vector (magnitude and direction) at the point x = 0.10 m. Use k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. (4 marks)
items.working:
Step 1 — Distances and directions:
- Point of interest is at x = 0.10 m.
- Distance to q1: r1 = 0.10 m (from x = 0.00 to 0.10). Field from q1 (positive) points away from q1, i.e. in +x direction.
- Distance to q2: r2 = 0.10 m (from x = 0.20 to 0.10). Field from q2 (negative) points toward q2, i.e. also in +x direction.

Step 2 — Magnitudes using E = k|q|/r^2:
- E1 = k * |q1| / r1^2 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2) * (3.0×10^-6 C) / (0.10 m)^2
     = 8.99×10^9 * 3.0×10^-6 / 0.01 N/C
     = 8.99×10^9 * 3.0×10^-4 N/C
     = 2.697×10^6 N/C.
- E2 = k * |q2| / r2^2 = (8.99×10^9) * (1.0×10^-6) / (0.10)^2
     = 8.99×10^9 * 1.0×10^-4 N/C
     = 8.99×10^5 N/C.

Step 3 — Vector sum (both in +x direction):
- E_net = E1 + E2 = 2.697×10^6 N/C + 8.99×10^5 N/C = 3.596×10^6 N/C.

Step 4 — Report to three significant figures and state direction:
- E_net ≈ 3.60×10^6 N/C in the +x (right) direction.

items.answer: On the metal sphere the added +2.0 μC spreads over the outer surface; on the plastic sphere the added +2.0 μC remains localized near the point where it was placed. Reason: In a conductor (metal) free electrons move until excess charge lies on the surface (here +2.0 μC = 2.0×10⁻⁶ C spread over the surface). In an insulator (plastic) charges cannot move freely, so the added charge stays where it was deposited.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This reverses the behaviours of conductors and insulators. A conductor does not keep extra charge localized because free electrons move; the plastic (insulator) does not let charge spread freely.
options.text: On the metal sphere the added +2.0 μC stays stuck near the point where it was placed; on the plastic sphere the charge spreads uniformly over the outer surface.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Correct — metals are conductors: free electrons move until excess charge resides on the outer surface (measurable as +2.0 μC distributed over the surface, in coulombs that is +2.0×10⁻⁶ C). Plastics are insulators: charges cannot move freely, so the added +2.0 μC stays localized near the application point.
options.text: On the metal sphere the added +2.0 μC spreads over the outer surface; on the plastic sphere the added +2.0 μC remains localized near the point where it was placed.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This choice assumes both materials allow charges to move freely. That is wrong because the plastic is an insulator and prevents free motion of charge so it does not generally form a uniform surface distribution.
options.text: On both the metal and the plastic spheres the added +2.0 μC spreads uniformly over their outer surfaces.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This choice assumes neither material allows charge to move. That is incorrect because metals are conductors: free charges will move and redistribute to the surface (so the metal will not keep the +2.0 μC stuck at the application point).
options.text: On both the metal and plastic spheres the added +2.0 μC remains trapped at the point of application and does not move.

items.stem: A single point charge Q = +5.0 μC is fixed at the origin. Calculate the electric field vector at the point P located at x = +0.20 m on the x-axis. Give the magnitude (in N C^-1) and the direction. (Take k = 8.99 × 10^9 N m^2 C^-2.)
items.working:
1. Write the electric field from a point charge: E = kQ / r^2, directed radially away from a positive charge.
2. Substitute values: Q = +5.0 μC = 5.0 × 10^-6 C, r = 0.20 m, k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2·C^-2.
   E = (8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2·C^-2) × (5.0 × 10^-6 C) / (0.20 m)^2.
3. Calculate denominator: (0.20 m)^2 = 0.0400 m^2.
   Numerator: (8.99 × 10^9) × (5.0 × 10^-6) = 44.95 × 10^3 = 4.495 × 10^4 (units: N·m^2·C^-1).
4. E = (4.495 × 10^4) / 0.0400 N C^-1 = 1.12375 × 10^6 N C^-1.
5. Round to three significant figures (given data to three s.f.): E = 1.12 × 10^6 N C^-1.
6. Direction: Q is positive, so the electric field at P (x = +0.20 m) points away from the charge, i.e. in the +x direction.
Final answer: E = 1.12 × 10^6 N C^-1, directed along +x.

items.answer:
(a) Electric field magnitude: E = kQ/r^2 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(5.0×10^-6 C)/(0.20 m)^2 = 1.12×10^6 N/C.

(b) Electric force on q: F = qE = (1.0×10^-9 C)(1.12×10^6 N/C) = 1.12×10^-3 N, directed radially outward from the source charge (repulsive since both charges are positive).

(c) The charge q is called a test charge because it probes the electric field produced by the source charge Q without significantly altering that field. q should be small compared with Q so that its own field does not appreciably move or change the source charge Q or the field configuration; this ensures the field measured depends only on the source charge.

rubric.criteria: Correct calculation of field and force; correct direction; clear explanation of why q is a test charge and must be small.

levels.descriptor: All parts correct: (a) E computed correctly with units and correct numeric value ≈ 1.12×10^6 N/C; (b) F computed correctly with units and correct numeric value ≈ 1.12×10^-3 N and direction stated as radially outward (repulsive); (c) concise correct explanation that q probes the field, defined by E = F/q, and q must be small so it does not appreciably alter the source charge or the field.
levels.label: Full marks

Example: correct E but wrong arithmetic in F (or vice versa), or correct numbers but missing units or slightly wrong by a factor of 2.5 or less.

items.stem:
A point source charge Q = +5.0 μC is fixed at the origin. (a) Calculate the electric field magnitude produced by Q at a distance r = 0.20 m from the origin. (b) A test charge q = +1.0 nC is placed at that location. Calculate the electric force on q and state its direction. (c) Briefly explain why q is called a test charge and why its magnitude should be small compared with Q when defining the electric field.

(Use k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Show all steps and include units.)
items.working:
(a) Compute E from a point charge formula, showing units stepwise:
Q = 5.0 μC = 5.0×10^-6 C
r = 0.20 m
k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2
E = kQ/r^2
  = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2) × (5.0×10^-6 C) / (0.20 m)^2
  = (8.99×10^9 × 5.0×10^-6) / 0.04  N/C
  = (8.99×5.0×10^3) / 0.04  N/C     [since 10^9 × 10^-6 = 10^3]
  = (44.95×10^3) / 0.04  N/C
  = 1.12375×10^6 N/C ≈ 1.12×10^6 N/C.

(b) q = 1.0 nC = 1.0×10^-9 C
F = qE = (1.0×10^-9 C)(1.12375×10^6 N/C)
  = 1.12375×10^-3 N ≈ 1.12×10^-3 N.
Direction: Both Q and q are positive, so the Coulomb force is repulsive; the force on q is radially outward from the origin.

(c) Explanation: The electric field E is defined as the force per unit test charge (E = F/q) produced by the source charge Q. To measure or define this field without changing it, the test charge q must be small so that its own electric field and the force it exerts on the source charge are negligible; otherwise the presence of q would alter the field that we aim to measure.

items.answer:
a) |E_P| : |E_Q| = 2 : 1 (i.e. |E_P| = 2|E_Q|).

b) The density of field lines leaving a charge represents the relative field strength; since A has twice as many lines leaving as B and the points are the same distance r, the field at P is twice that at Q. The absolute number of drawn field lines is not a fixed physical property — the artist can choose how many lines to draw, so only the relative density (lines per unit area around the charge) indicates relative field strength.

items.stem:
Two isolated positive point charges, A and B, are drawn with field-line diagrams. Around charge A eight equally spaced field lines leave the charge; around charge B four equally spaced field lines leave the charge. Point P is at distance r from charge A along one of its field lines. Point Q is at the same distance r from charge B along one of its field lines. (a) Calculate the ratio of the magnitudes of the electric fields |E_P| : |E_Q| at P and Q. (b) Give a brief physical explanation (one or two sentences) that justifies this ratio and addresses whether the absolute number of drawn field lines is a fixed physical property of the charge.

(Mark allocation: 2 marks for the numeric ratio, 2 marks for the explanation.)
items.working:
Step 1: Use the rule that, in field-line diagrams, the local field magnitude is proportional to the local density of field lines (lines per unit area through a surface around the charge).

Step 2: At the same radial distance r, and along a single field line, the local density around A is proportional to the number of lines leaving A (8) and around B proportional to the number leaving B (4), assuming equal spacing.

Step 3: Ratio |E_P|/|E_Q| = (number of lines from A)/(number of lines from B) = 8/4 = 2.

Therefore |E_P| : |E_Q| = 2 : 1, so |E_P| = 2|E_Q|.

Units: electric field in newtons per coulomb (N C^-1), but ratio is dimensionless.
