entry_ticket.expected_response: Net total charge = +2e. After touching, charge redistributes between the two identical spheres so each ends with +1e on average, or one way answer: each sphere has +1e (so A = +1e, B = +1e). Reason: charge is conserved and redistributes when conductors touch.
entry_ticket.prompt: You have two small identical metal spheres, A has +3e and B has -1e (e = 1.60×10^-19 C). You touch them together and then separate them. What is the net charge on A and B after separation, in units of e? Briefly explain one sentence why.

exit_ticket.prompt: A small paper square is given a net charge of −2.4×10^-17 C. (a) How many extra electrons does it carry? (b) Write the result both as an integer number of electrons and as the same charge in units of e. Show units and brief working.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student calculates n = q/e = (−2.4×10^-17 C)/(−1.60×10^-19 C) = 150 electrons, states the sign (extra electrons: 150), and shows the charge as −150 e or −150 × e = −2.4×10^-17 C with units.

homework.submission_format: Hand in a single sheet with calculations and the short written explanation; clearly label each part (a),(b),(c) and include units.
tasks: Convert each charge to a number of elementary charges and state the sign (extra electrons or deficit): (a) +4.8×10^-19 C, (b) −8.0×10^-18 C, (c) +1.0×10^-6 C. Show work with q = n e and include units.
Two identical metal spheres carry charges of +8e and +2e. They touch and are separated. Calculate the final charge on each sphere in elementary charges and in coulombs.

Short written explanation (3–5 sentences): Explain why charge appears to be 'lost' when an object is neutralised by contact, and correct the misconception by stating what actually happens to electrons and the net charge of the isolated system.

mentor_moment.story: A student once rubbed a plastic comb on their sleeve, then noticed it picked up tiny paper bits. They counted this as 'magic' until we calculated the comb carried about 10^12 extra electrons — a huge number compared with atoms but a tiny fraction of the comb's electrons.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Even a small measurable charge corresponds to trillions of electrons moving; that helps make abstract charges feel concrete when you attach numbers and units.
mentor_moment.title: The Coin and the Comb

anticipated_questions: If they neutralise, how can the total stay the same?
Can one sphere end up with more than +3e after touching?
Do we have to count electrons only, or protons too?
teacher_script.board_action: Write two columns labelled 'Answer from students' and 'Why?'. Copy one typical wrong answer: 'charges destroyed' and one correct: 'redistributed, conserved'.
teacher_script.heading: Warm-up and surface prior ideas
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Read the ticket. Put a short answer on the board: what are the charges on A and B after they touch? One line explanation." Walk quickly while students write. After 90 seconds, ask one student with an answer to read theirs. If a student says 'charges disappear' or 'they cancel and go to zero' ask: 'What do you mean by disappear? Where did the electrons go?' Collect 2–3 different answers aloud. Say: 'We'll test that idea today.'

anticipated_questions: Why does it spread evenly? (Because they're identical conductors and charges move until equilibrium.)
Why do we use e and not count protons? (Free charge transfer is electrons; protons stay in nuclei.)
What if one sphere is bigger? (Charge divides in proportion to capacity — beyond today's scope.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw two circles labelled S1 (rubbed) and S2 (neutral). Next to S1 write '-5e' and compute '-5 × 1.60×10^-19 C = -8.0×10^-19 C' showing the multiplication and unit 'C'. Arrow between spheres showing 'touch → redistribute'.
teacher_script.heading: Demonstration and measurement (rubbing and counting idea)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "I'll show a quick demo with two pith-ball-like spheres drawn here and a cloth. When I rub the cloth on the right sphere it gains electrons; the left is left neutral." Point to diagram. Ask: 'If the rubbed sphere gains -5e, what is its charge in coulombs? Use e = 1.60×10^-19 C.' Wait for a volunteer to compute: -5 × 1.60×10^-19 C = -8.0×10^-19 C. Write the arithmetic step as you say it. Then say: 'Now if those two spheres touch and are identical conductors, charge spreads evenly. What happens to the number of elementary charges? Does the total number change?' Pause for answers and emphasise: 'Total number of excess electrons stays the same — conservation.'

anticipated_questions: But you said n must be an integer — so how can we get −12.5? (Answer: measurement precision; real objects have integer n, measurement rounding gives non-integer.)
Can n be positive? (Yes: positive n means missing electrons, net positive charge.)
Why is e the same for all electrons? (Elementary charge is the magnitude of electron/proton charge.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write: 'q = n e' then beneath: 'q (C) ÷ e (C) = n (unitless integer)'. Show the sample division: (−2.0×10^-18 C) ÷ (1.60×10^-19 C) = −12.5 → approximately −12 or −13 electrons depending on rounding/precision.
teacher_script.heading: Derive q = n e from counting electrons
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We can describe any net free charge as a number of elementary charges times e. Write the relation with me: q = n e. Here q is the measured charge in coulombs, n is an integer (can be negative), and e = 1.60×10^-19 C. Example: if 2.0×10^-18 C of extra negative charge is measured, what is n?" Wait for calculation: n = q/e = (−2.0×10^-18 C)/(1.60×10^-19 C) = −12.5. Point out: "n must be an integer for an isolated object with free charges. So a measured q like −2.0×10^-18 C would mean about −12 or −13 electrons extra; the exact integer depends on measurement precision. For classroom problems we keep numbers that divide cleanly." Emphasise units each step: 'C divided by C gives unitless n.'

anticipated_questions: Why did we divide by e to get n? (Because q = n e, so n = q/e.)
If q is very small, can n be zero? (Yes; zero net excess charge means n = 0.)
What if q is not a multiple of e exactly? (Measurement/rounding; physical n is integer.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the three problems and solve #1 and #2 step-by-step with units. For #3 write: '+6e + (−2e) = +4e → each sphere → +2e'.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: convert and check conservation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out or project three quick problems and solve the first together aloud: 1) A rod has +4e. What is q in C? 2) A particle has q = −3.2×10^-19 C. How many elementary charges is that? 3) Two spheres, one with +6e one with −2e touch — what are final charges on each if identical? For (1) say: q = n e = 4 × 1.60×10^-19 C = 6.4×10^-19 C. Write each step and the unit. For (2) compute n = q/e = −3.2×10^-19 / 1.60×10^-19 = −2 → answer: −2e. For (3) total = +4e; after touching each has +2e. Ask students to do these in pairs for 4 minutes and write answers; circulate and correct work.

anticipated_questions: If opposite charges cancel, why don't they disappear from the universe? (They combine to make neutral atoms but the electrons and protons remain; net charge is conserved.)
When they neutralise is energy released? (Yes, sometimes as light/heat — not required today.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the quick question, then the correct arithmetic: '−8e = −8 × 1.60×10^-19 C = −1.28×10^-18 C' and one sentence: 'Conservation: electrons moved from rod to conductor; total charge of system unchanged.'
teacher_script.heading: Formative check — quick quiz and misconceptions
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Give one quick written question: 'A neutral conductor touches a rod with −8e. After separation, what is the charge on the conductor (in C)? Explain in one sentence how conservation works here.' Collect answers quickly or have students hold up a card with their answer. If many show '0' or 'disappeared', say: 'No — charges aren't destroyed. The conductor gained −8e overall; that's −8 × 1.60×10^-19 C = −1.28×10^-18 C.' Reiterate: 'When opposite charges meet they neutralise locally, but the total charge of the isolated system is conserved.'

anticipated_questions: Can we use 1.6×10^-19 for e instead of 1.60×10^-19? (Yes, but keep consistent significant figures.)
Will we need Coulomb's law today? (No — it's listed for the course but not used in calculations today.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write 'Homework: 3 problems — conversions and one touching conductors. Due next lesson.'
teacher_script.heading: Consolidation and homework
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Summarise aloud: 'We saw charge is q = n e with e = 1.60×10^-19 C, and we must keep units. Touching conductors redistributes charge but the total number of excess elementary charges stays the same. For homework: three problems — convert between n and q, and one touching conductors problem similar to today's. Due next lesson.' Hand out the sheet or write assignment on board.

bullet_points: e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C (elementary charge magnitude)
Conductor: charges move and redistribute → excess on surface
Insulator: charges stay where placed (localized)
Electric field (operational): force on a unit positive test charge placed at the point; equivalently force per unit test charge
Units: force in newtons (N), charge in coulombs (C), field in N/C
Superposition: net electrostatic force = vector sum of pairwise forces (each pairwise force unchanged by others)
Takeaway: Use n·e to convert e-units to C; E = F / q to get field; always include units
diagrams_to_draw: Sketch: metal sphere with + signs spread over outer surface; label 'conductor'
Sketch: plastic rod with + signs clumped in one spot; label 'insulator'
Sketch: +Q1 (left) and +Q2 (right) with q_t between; arrows showing F1, F2 on q_t and resulting F_net

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Compute n = q / e = (3.204 × 10^-19 C) / (1.602 × 10^-19 C) = 2. So n = +2 (two positive elementary charges). The object has an excess of two protons (or is missing two electrons). Include units and the division step.
checkpoint_questions.question: A tiny object carries charge q = +3.204 × 10^-19 C. Using q = n e with e = 1.602 × 10^-19 C, find n (the number of elementary charges) and state whether the object has excess protons or electrons.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: On the metal sphere (a conductor) the extra negative charge redistributes and resides entirely on the surface. On the plastic rod (an insulator) the extra charge stays localized near where it was placed and does not move freely. Reason: in a conductor free electrons move until they reach the surface; in an insulator electrons are bound and cannot move freely.
checkpoint_questions.question: You have a metal sphere and a plastic rod, each given the same net negative charge. Where does that extra negative charge reside on the metal sphere and on the plastic rod? Give one physical reason (in one sentence) for the difference.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Field from +2e at origin points to the right (away from +), magnitude k(2e)/(0.10^2). Field from −2e also points to the right (toward −), same magnitude. Net field = 2 × k(2e)/(0.10^2) to the right = (4 k e)/(0.10^2). Numerically: 4 × 8.99×10^9 × 1.602×10^-19 / 0.01 ≈ 5.8×10^-7 N/C to the right. Show vector direction and units.
checkpoint_questions.question: Two point charges lie on the x-axis: +2e at x = -0.10 m and −2e at x = +0.10 m. Use superposition to find the direction and magnitude of the electric field at the origin (x = 0). (Use k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2 and e = 1.602 × 10^-19 C.)

entry_ticket.expected_response: Calculation: q = 3 × (1.60 × 10^-19 C) = 4.8 × 10^-19 C. Answer: 4.8 × 10^-19 C. If a student writes 'impossible' they should say they don't know the value of e.
entry_ticket.prompt: Write a short answer (2 lines max): A small plastic rod was rubbed with wool and now has a net charge of +3e. What is that charge in coulombs? Show one calculation step and give the number with units. If you think it is impossible to answer, write why.

exit_ticket.prompt: A small dust grain has measured charge q = −4.806 × 10^-19 C. Using q = n e with e = 1.602 × 10^-19 C, compute n and explain in one sentence what that integer means physically.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Shows n = q/e = (−4.806×10^-19 C)/(1.602×10^-19 C) = −3, includes units and the arithmetic, and states that the grain carries a net charge of −3 elementary charges (three extra electrons).

homework.submission_format: One page of written answers (handwritten or typed) or a single PDF with calculations and short explanations.
tasks: Convert each of these charges into an integer number of elementary charges (n) and show the arithmetic: (a) q = +8.01 × 10^-19 C, (b) q = −1.602 × 10^-18 C, (c) q = +1.0 × 10^-21 C. State whether each result is physically allowed (integer) or indicates a measurement rounding.

Two equal small metal balls are isolated and then touched together so charge can move. Before contact ball A had +5e and ball B had −1e. After separating them, what is the charge on each ball? Show the conservation-of-charge calculation in elementary charges and in coulombs (use e = 1.602 × 10^-19 C).

Short answer (one paragraph): Explain how you would use a small positive test charge to determine the direction of the electric field at a point near a charged insulating rod, mentioning what you must ensure so the test charge does not disturb the source charge distribution.

mentor_moment.story: In a lab I once measured a tiny bead with q ≈ −1.602×10^-18 C and first panicked; dividing by e showed it was exactly −10e. Realizing the charge was an integer made the result sensible and saved time troubleshooting the apparatus.
mentor_moment.takeaway: When a measured charge looks odd, divide by e and check whether you get a small integer — that often reveals measurement rounding or a correct quantised result.
mentor_moment.title: Counting Charges in the Lab

anticipated_questions: Why is e written with a lowercase letter? (Because e is the magnitude of the electron charge; it's a defined constant.)
Can n be negative? (Yes — n is negative if the net charge has more electrons than protons.)
Do we need more than 2 significant figures for e? (Use 1.60 × 10^-19 C here; we'll keep that precision.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the example students did: 'Example: +3e -> ? C' then write 'e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C' and the single worked calculation line '3 × 1.60 × 10^-19 C = 4.8 × 10^-19 C'.
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge: check quantisation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Read the entry ticket aloud: 'A rod has charge +3e. What is that in coulombs?' Wait 30 seconds for students to finish. Ask one student to read their calculation step and number. If a student writes 'impossible', ask: 'What number would let us compute this? (Expect: value of e.)' Repeat if necessary: point to the printed constant on the sheet: e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C. Tell class: 'Today we will use that relation again; we must always write units.'

anticipated_questions: Does every metal conduct equally well? (No — conductivity differs, but all conductors allow charge to move compared to insulators.)
What about semiconductors? (Not covered today; they are in between.)
Do neutral conductors have charges on the surface? (If net charge is zero, there is no excess on the surface; only when charged do we get excess on the surface.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw two labeled sketches: a circle labeled 'metal (conductor)' with + signs spread on outer surface; a rod labeled 'plastic (insulator)' with + signs clumped. Write two short bullets: 'Conductor: charges move and redistribute (surface).' and 'Insulator: charges stay where placed (localized).'
teacher_script.heading: Introduce conductors vs insulators
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Hold the metal water bottle in your hand.' Pause. 'Metals are conductors: electrons can move freely through them.' Point to a plastic ruler and say: 'Plastic is an insulator: charges we put on it stay where we put them.' Draw a quick physical example: a metal sphere and a plastic rod. Ask: 'If I touch a charged metal sphere, where do the charges go?' Let students answer. If no answer: 'They spread over the surface.' Then demonstrate with a picture: mark + charges spreading over the outer surface of the sphere and on the rod mark a few + charges in one spot to show localization. Emphasize units: 'Charge measured in coulombs.' Finally ask: 'Which would let charges move to the outside when charged, conductor or insulator?' Confirm: conductor.

anticipated_questions: Why use a positive test charge? (A positive test charge gives the direction of the field in the usual sense; if you used a negative test charge the force would be opposite.)
What does 'without disturbing the source charges' mean? (The test charge must be small enough that it does not change the arrangement of the source charges.)
Is electric field a vector? (Yes — magnitude and direction matter; we showed direction 'to the right'.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the operational definition exactly as given. Then write the numeric worked example: 'Given: F = 6.0×10^-3 N on q_t = 2.0 μC (2.0×10^-6 C). E = F / q_t = 6.0×10^-3 N ÷ 2.0×10^-6 C = 3.0×10^3 N/C (direction: right).' Include units N/C.
teacher_script.heading: Operational definition: electric field
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Now we define electric field by an experiment.' Place an imagined small positive test charge q_t at a point P near a source charge +Q. Ask: 'What do we measure there?' Guide students to say 'a force on the test charge.' State the operational definition exactly: 'The electric field at a point is the force experienced by a unit positive test charge placed there (without disturbing the source charges); equivalently, force per unit test charge.' Now place numbers: 'If a 2.0 μC test charge experiences a force of 6.0 × 10^-3 N to the right at P, what is the field at P?' Pause for calculation. Lead them through: E = F / q_t, show units: N / C. Compute: 6.0 × 10^-3 N ÷ 2.0 × 10^-6 C = 3.0 × 10^3 N/C to the right. Emphasize 'unit positive test charge' and 'without disturbing the source charges' by asking what would happen if the test charge were large (it would change the source charges — not allowed for the definition).

anticipated_questions: Why can we just add forces? (Because electrostatic forces follow the superposition principle; each pairwise force is calculated as if other charges were not present.)
Do we need vectors? (Yes — direction matters; if forces are opposite we subtract magnitudes.)
What if the charges are not pointlike? (Today's examples use point-like or small localized charges; distribution issues come later.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw the diagram with +Q1, +Q2, and q_t. Write bullet: 'Superposition: F_net = F_1 + F_2 (vector sum).' Then write the numeric steps showing q values in coulombs (convert using n·e in words), the given pairwise forces, the sum, and E_net = F_net / q_t with the final number and units N/C.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce superposition for forces and link to field
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Draw two source charges on the board: +Q1 at left and +Q2 at right, and a small positive test charge q_t at a point between them. Ask: 'What is the net force on q_t?' Let students suggest 'add the forces from each charge.' Say: 'That is the principle of superposition: the net electrostatic force equals the vector sum of the forces from each source, and each pairwise force is unchanged by the others.' Work one simple numeric example: Q1 = +2e (so compute in coulombs), Q2 = +1e, place q_t = +1e at a point where force magnitudes from each are 4.8×10^-20 N left and 2.4×10^-20 N right respectively (use these numbers). Ask students to compute net force and direction: net = 4.8×10^-20 N left minus 2.4×10^-20 N right = 2.4×10^-20 N left. Then show how to get net field by dividing net force by q_t: E_net = F_net / q_t — here q_t = 1e = 1.60×10^-19 C — compute E_net in N/C with units. Do the arithmetic aloud and write each step; keep units visible.

anticipated_questions: How did you get 3.2×10^-19 C for 2e? (Multiply 2 × 1.60×10^-19 C.)
Why is the field smaller than the force? (Because field is force divided by the test charge; large test charge gives smaller E for same F.)
Why is the sign negative for -5e? (Negative means an excess of electrons; the numerical value with sign gives direction for forces on positive test charges.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the two-part questions and leave space for student answers. After presentations, write the correct answers with calculation lines: '-5e = -8.0×10^-19 C' and 'E = F/q = 1.6×10^-19 N ÷ 3.2×10^-19 C = 0.50 N/C upward' (showing q = 2e = 3.20×10^-19 C).
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: compute charge and field
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Give a quick two-part pair task (2 minutes): Part A: Convert -5e to coulombs. Part B: A test charge of +2e feels a force of 1.6×10^-19 N upward. What is the field at that point? Tell pairs: 'Write answers and one line of calculation; I'll call on two pairs.' Circulate, correct notation and units. Call on one pair to present both answers. If they make arithmetic slip, write corrected steps on the board and ask class to spot the mistake.

anticipated_questions: Will we need to memorize e exactly? (Yes — use 1.60×10^-19 C here; more precision not needed for these problems.)
How do we know when to divide by q to get E versus summing fields? (You can divide the net force by q or sum the fields from each source; both give the same E.)
teacher_script.board_action: Underline the main points already on the board. Add one final bullet: 'Takeaway: q in C (use n·e); E = F/q (N/C); superposition = vector sum; conductors: surface; insulators: localized.'
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding and consolidate
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask two quick checks aloud: 1) 'If a conductor is charged, where will excess charges end up?' Students answer: 'on the surface.' 2) 'If two charges both push a test charge, how do we find the total force?' Students: 'Add the vector forces (superposition).' Summarize: 'We used q = n e to get coulombs, defined E = F/q operationally, and used superposition to get net force or field. Next period we will treat source vs test charge more formally and compute flux.' End by asking students to keep today's board notes in their notebook.

bullet_points: Electric field (operational): force on a unit positive test charge placed at the point (without disturbing the source charges); equivalently, force per unit test charge. Units: N/C.
Superposition: E_net = vector sum of fields from each source charge evaluated at the point.
Flux through element: dΦ = E · dS = E dS cosθ (θ = angle between E and area normal). Units: N·m^2/C.
Dipole: two equal and opposite point charges ±q separated by 2a. Dipole moment p = q 2a, directed from -q to +q. Units: C·m.
Quantisation: q = n e. Use e = 1.6×10^-19 C for calculations.
diagrams_to_draw: Point source charge (label +Q) with a small positive test charge at a nearby point; arrow showing force on test charge.
Two point charges on x-axis: +2.0×10^-6 C at x=-0.10 m and -1.0×10^-6 C at x=+0.10 m. Show field vectors at origin and arrows indicating directions.
Tiny surface element dS (square) with area normal arrow; show E making 60° with normal and the projection E cosθ through the area.
Dipole: -q at left, +q at right, separation labelled 2a; arrow from -q to +q labelled p.
headings: Electric Flux through a surface element

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Both charges produce fields on the x-axis. At x = 1.0 cm the field from the + charge (at 0) points away from origin (toward +x) and the field from the - charge (at 2.0 cm) points toward the negative charge (also toward +x). They add in the +x direction, so the net E points +x. (Student should note both contributions point same way and add.)
checkpoint_questions.question: A +4.8 × 10^-19 C point charge sits at the origin and a -4.8 × 10^-19 C point charge sits at x = 2.0 cm. Using the operational definition of E, what is the direction and sense (toward/away) of the net electric field at the point x = 1.0 cm on the x-axis? Show reasoning in one line.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: dPhi = E dS cosθ. Numerically: Φ = (200 N/C)(0.020 m^2)cos60° = 200×0.020×0.5 = 2.0 N·m^2/C. (Include units N·m^2/C.)
checkpoint_questions.question: Write the expression for the electric flux through a flat square of area 0.020 m^2 when a uniform field of magnitude 200 N/C passes through it at 60° from the area normal. Calculate the numerical flux with units.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: p = q·2a = (2.0×1.602×10^-19 C)×(0.010 m) = 3.204×10^-21 C·m (≈3.2×10^-21 C·m). Direction: from the negative charge to the positive charge.
checkpoint_questions.question: A dipole consists of +2.0e and -2.0e separated by 1.0 cm (so 2a = 1.0 cm). Give the dipole moment magnitude in coulomb·meter and state its direction using the definition in the lesson.

entry_ticket.expected_response: B — The paper remains neutral overall but is polarised: charges separate so the nearer side is opposite in sign to the comb and attracted, giving a net attraction without net charge transfer.
entry_ticket.prompt:
A plastic comb picks up small neutral bits of paper after you run it through your hair. Circle the best explanation and give one short sentence to justify it:

A) The paper became net charged by touching the comb.
B) The paper is still neutral but has its positive and negative charges moved slightly apart (induced dipole), and the comb attracts it.
C) The paper produces its own electric field that pulls the comb in.

Write the letter and one sentence.

exit_ticket.prompt: An object carries a net charge of -9.6 × 10^-19 C. Using q = n e, (a) how many excess elementary charges n does the object have (give sign and integer or nearest integer), and (b) express that charge as a multiple of e (e.g., -3 e). Show the short calculation.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student divides charge by elementary charge e = 1.602×10^-19 C to get n ≈ -6.00 (so n = -6 excess electrons) and writes the charge as -6 e or -9.6×10^-19 C = (-6)(1.602×10^-19 C).

homework.submission_format: Hand in one page with numbered solutions; show all steps and units.
tasks: 1) Convert the following numbers of elementary charges to coulombs (give answers in C): (a) +1.0×10^6 e, (b) -3 e, (c) +12 e. Show the division by e = 1.602×10^-19 C.

2) Three point charges lie on the x-axis: +2.0×10^-19 C at x=0, -1.0×10^-19 C at x=3.0 cm, +1.0×10^-19 C at x=6.0 cm. Compute the net electric field (magnitude and direction) at x=9.0 cm by vector superposition; show intermediate values and units (N/C).

3) A uniform electric field of 150 N/C is perpendicular to a circular disk of radius 4.0 cm. (a) Calculate the flux through the disk. (b) If the same field is tilted so the angle between E and the area normal is 30°, what is the new flux? Show formulas and units.

mentor_moment.story: I once rubbed a plastic comb and watched tiny bits of paper jump up. The comb didn't give the paper a net charge; the comb's field pulled the paper's charges slightly apart (an induced dipole), and the nearer opposite charges felt a stronger pull, so the paper stuck.
mentor_moment.takeaway: A neutral object can be attracted without net charging: induced dipoles in a non-uniform field produce a net force toward the charged object.
mentor_moment.title: Comb, paper and induced dipoles

anticipated_questions: But how can one side be more attracted if the paper has equal positive and negative charges?
Does the comb give charge to the paper when we touch it?
Is polarization permanent?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the entry ticket question's key wording on the board and underline the correct choice B.
teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets; brief class read-aloud
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Take 2 minutes to finish your entry ticket and hand it to me when you're done." Walk the room quickly reading a few responses aloud: choose one that wrote A, one that wrote B. Then say: "If you wrote A, tell us why you thought the paper got a net charge." Pause for 1 quick student answer. Then say: "If you wrote B, say how the charges are arranged in the paper." Pause for 1 quick answer. Conclude: "Good — today we'll see why a neutral object can be attracted without gaining net charge: induced dipoles and how we describe fields and flux."

anticipated_questions: How small must a test charge be?
If the test charge moves, does it change the field?
Why use a positive test charge?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the operational definition sentence exactly from the source and below it write units: E = N/C.
teacher_script.heading: Operational definition of electric field and source/test charges
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We need a clear definition: place a tiny positive test charge at a point and measure the force on it without moving the source charges. The electric field is that force per unit positive charge." Put a small toy ball labelled +q_test and a larger fixed charged object on the desk as a physical anchor. Ask: "Which is the source charge and which is the test charge here?" Wait for answer. Then say: "The source charge must be treated as fixed; we only measure how a tiny test charge would feel a force there." Emphasize units: "Force in newtons divided by charge in coulombs gives E in newtons per coulomb (N/C)."

anticipated_questions: Why did both fields point the same way when one charge is negative?
Where did the value k = 9.0×10^9 come from?
What if the point wasn't on the line between charges?
teacher_script.board_action: Draw the two point charges with coordinates and arrows showing each field at the origin. Write the numerical calculation lines with k = 9.0×10^9 N·m^2/C^2 and show E1 = 1.8×10^6 N/C, E2 = 9.0×10^5 N/C, E_net = 2.7×10^6 N/C to the right.
teacher_script.heading: Superposition principle (vector sum of fields)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "If there are several point source charges, the net electric field at a point is the vector sum of the fields each source would produce there. We'll do a quick two-charge example." Draw two point charges on the board: +2e-6 C at x = -0.10 m and -1e-6 C at x = +0.10 m. Ask: "At the origin, what is the direction of the field from each charge?" Pause for answers: left / right. Then compute magnitudes step by step: show Coulomb's law verbally: 'force ~ 1/r^2' but do not write new formulas beyond allowed. Use numeric values: distance from each to origin is 0.10 m; compute E1 = k*2e-6/(0.10^2) and E2 = k*1e-6/(0.10^2). Use k = 9.0×10^9 N·m^2/C^2 and show units. Calculate numbers: E1 = (9.0e9*2e-6)/(0.01) = (18e3)/0.01? Wait compute: 9e9*2e-6 = 18e3 = 1.8e4; divide by 0.01 gives 1.8e6 N/C. Similarly E2 = 9e9*1e-6/0.01 = 9e3/0.01 = 9e5? Check: 9e9*1e-6 = 9e3 = 9000; /0.01 = 900000 = 9e5 N/C. So net field is E_net = E1 (to right because + charge repels positive test?) Wait sign careful: At origin, +2e-6 at left (-0.1) pushes positive test to right. -1e-6 at +0.1 attracts positive test to right as well. Both to right, so add magnitudes: 1.8e6 + 9e5 = 2.7e6 N/C to the right. Say each arithmetic step aloud and write short lines of the computation, keeping units. Ask: "What does superposition mean here?" Summarize: "Vector add component-wise if not collinear."

anticipated_questions: What are the units of flux?
What does negative flux mean physically?
How small must dS be for this formula to be valid?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the flux formula exactly: dΦ = E · dS = E dS cosθ. Draw the surface element with normal, draw E at 60°, and show the numeric substitution and arithmetic leading to dΦ = 2.0 N·m^2/C.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce electric flux through a surface element
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Flux tells us how many field lines pass through a surface. For a tiny surface element dS, flux dΦ = E · dS = E dS cosθ where θ is angle between E and the area normal." Point to the board formula. Draw a small square surface element with a normal arrow and a field vector at an angle. Ask: "If E is parallel to the normal, what is cosθ and what is the flux sign?" Wait for 'cosθ = 1, flux positive'. Ask: "If E is perpendicular to the normal?" Wait for 'flux zero.' Then do a quick numerical example: choose E = 2.0×10^4 N/C, area dS = 2.0×10^-4 m^2, θ = 60°. Compute dΦ = E dS cos60° = 2.0×10^4 * 2.0×10^-4 * 0.5. Do arithmetic aloud: 2.0×10^4 * 2.0×10^-4 = 4.0×10^0 = 4.0; times 0.5 = 2.0. So dΦ = 2.0 (units: N·m^2/C). Write units explicitly. Emphasize interpretation: "Positive flux means field leaves through the surface in the direction of the area normal."

anticipated_questions: Why point from negative to positive, not the other way?
Is p a vector? What if charges are vertical?
How does induced dipole strength depend on the material?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the dipole definition sentence exactly and the formula p = q 2a. Under it write the numerical steps: q = 3×1.6×10^-19 = 4.8×10^-19 C; p = 4.8×10^-19 × 2.0×10^-9 = 9.6×10^-28 C·m. Draw a dipole diagram: -q at left, +q at right, arrow labelled p pointing right.
teacher_script.heading: Define electric dipole and quick calculation using quantisation q = n e
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "A dipole is two equal and opposite point charges +q and -q separated by 2a. The dipole moment p = q×2a and points from negative to positive." Point to the board definition. Give a concrete example: let q = 3 e (three elementary charges). Ask: "What is q in coulombs?" Wait for a student to say multiply by e = 1.6×10^-19 C. Do it: q = 3 × 1.6×10^-19 C = 4.8×10^-19 C. Next choose 2a = 2.0×10^-9 m (separation). Compute magnitude p = q×2a = 4.8×10^-19 C × 2.0×10^-9 m = 9.6×10^-28 C·m. Write units. Emphasize direction arrow from - to +. Ask: "Why does a neutral object stuck to a charged comb not require net charge?" Link back to induced dipole: one side slightly more negative than the other so the comb attracts it. If time, demonstrate with small pieces of paper and a charged comb (safety permitting).

anticipated_questions: Why did we pick the test charge positive in the definition?
Can flux be larger than the field value times area?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the two worksheet questions on the board. After students work, write the solutions: q = 1×1.6×10^-19 = 1.6×10^-19 C; p = q×0.10 = 1.6×10^-20 C·m. Flux = E dS cos0 = 5.0×10^3 × 1.0×10^-4 = 0.50 N·m^2/C.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice and rapid consolidation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out a 2-question worksheet (or display on the board): (1) A point -1e charges at x=0.05 m and +1e at x=0.05 m; find q in C and p if separation 2a = 0.10 m. (2) A small surface element has area 1.0×10^-4 m^2, E = 5.0×10^3 N/C perpendicular to the surface normal. Compute flux. Give students 4 minutes to work and circulate. After 4 minutes, call the class back and write the answers step-by-step on the board, asking students to tell the next arithmetic step. End with: "What is one thing you will remember from today?" Have 1-2 students answer briefly.

anticipated_questions: Will we have homework on this?
Will we calculate dipole fields in detail next time?
teacher_script.board_action: Write two final prompts: 'Define dipole moment (one sentence)' and 'Units of flux and dipole moment'.
teacher_script.heading: Exit check and link to next lesson
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Quick check: in one sentence, what is the dipole moment and what are its units?" Call on 2 students. Then say: "Next time we'll compare how dipole fields fall off with distance compared to single charges and begin Gauss's law applications. Tonight, read the first paragraph on dipole field fall-off if you can." Collect any remaining worksheets as students leave.

bullet_points: Dipole: two opposite charges +q and −q separated by 2a, center at origin.
For point on axis at x = r with r >> a, distances: R+ = r − a, R− = r + a (units: m).
Add point-charge fields and expand in a/r to leading order: E ∝ p/(4πϵ0 r^3) with p = q(2a) (p in C·m).
Dipole field falls off as 1/r^3 for r >> a (not 1/r^2).
Coulomb's law (point charges): F = (1/4πϵ0) (q1 q2 / r^2) r̂  (N, C, m).
Gauss's law (integral): Φ_E = ∮ E · dS = q_enc / ϵ0.
Infinite line charge example: choose cylinder coaxial with line. Flux through curved surface = E(2π r L). Enclosed q = λ L.
Solve: E = λ/(2πϵ0 r) (units: λ in C/m, E in N/C).
Charge quantisation: q = n e, with e = 1.60×10^-19 C. Example: 20e = 3.20×10^-18 C.
diagrams_to_draw: Diagram: x-axis with −q at x=−a and +q at x=+a; point at x=r labelled r (r >> a).
Diagram: cylindrical Gaussian surface around an infinite line-charge (show radius r and length L).
Small table of sensor readings vs distance for demo (r = 5 cm, 10 cm, 20 cm) with ratios.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: n = q/e = (-3.2×10^-19 C)/(1.60×10^-19 C) = -2. So n = -2, which is an integer: the charge equals the charge of two electrons, so it is physically possible.
checkpoint_questions.question: A particle carries charge q = -3.2 × 10^-19 C. Using q = n e where e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C, find n (the number of elementary charges) and say whether this q could come from an integer number of electrons.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Dipole field scales as 1/r^3 so E2 = E1 × (r1/r2)^3 = 2.0×10^-6 N/C × (1.0/2.0)^3 = 2.0×10^-6 N/C × 1/8 = 2.5×10^-7 N/C. Units remain N/C.
checkpoint_questions.question: At points far from a dipole (distance r much larger than dipole half-separation a), the dipole electric field scales roughly as 1/r^3. Suppose at r = 1.0 m the field magnitude is E1 = 2.0 × 10^-6 N/C. Estimate the field at r = 2.0 m and show the reasoning with units.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Flux Φ = E × (curved area) = E × (2π r L). Enclosed charge q_enc = λ L (λ in C/m). Gauss's law: E(2π r L) = q_enc/ε0 = λ L/ε0. Cancel L: E(r) = λ/(2π ε0 r). Units: λ [C/m], ε0 [C^2/(N·m^2)] so E [N/C].
checkpoint_questions.question: You choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface coaxial with an infinite line charge of linear charge density λ. Write the Gauss's law equation that relates the magnitude E on the curved surface to the enclosed charge and solve algebraically for E(r) (show units for λ and E).

entry_ticket.expected_response: Circle 1/r^3. Reason (short): At large r the +q and −q nearly cancel their 1/r^2 fields, leaving a weaker field that falls off like 1/r^3; the field depends on the dipole moment p = q(2a).
entry_ticket.prompt: Look at a pair of equal and opposite point charges +q and −q separated by 2a on the x-axis, centered at the origin. At a point far away on the +x axis (distance r from origin, with r >> a), do you expect the electric field magnitude to fall off like 1/r^2 or 1/r^3? Circle one and write one short sentence giving your reason.

exit_ticket.prompt: A small bead has total charge q = +4.8 × 10^-19 C. (a) Express this charge as n times the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C and give n with sign. (b) State in one sentence whether this q could come from an integer number of protons or electrons and why.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Shows calculation n = q/e = (4.8×10^-19)/(1.60×10^-19) = +3 and states that yes: n = +3 is an integer so the charge could come from three excess protons (or a deficit of three electrons).

homework.submission_format: scan or clear photo of handwritten work or a single typed PDF
tasks: Convert each listed charge into the integer number of elementary charges n and into coulombs if needed: (a) +1.60×10^-19 C, (b) -4.8×10^-19 C, (c) +8.0×10^-21 C. Show the division q/e with units and state whether each is physically an integer multiple of e.
Estimate the number of electrons that make up a net charge of -1.0 μC (microcoulomb). Show the calculation and give the answer in scientific notation.
A dipole has charges ±q separated by 2a. If at r = 0.50 m the dipole field magnitude is 8.0×10^-6 N/C, estimate the field at r = 1.50 m using the 1/r^3 scaling and show units.

mentor_moment.story: In a lab, a student expected tiny charges like 10^-19 C to be measurement noise, then found their value was exactly -2e after division by e and recognized two missing electrons from a transfer. That integer result made the tiny number meaningful.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Whenever you get a tiny charge, divide by e and check for an integer — an exact integer tells you how many elementary charges were transferred.
mentor_moment.title: Small numbers, big meaning

anticipated_questions: Why would the fields cancel? Aren't they different signs so they always cancel?
If charges are equal and opposite, shouldn't the field always be zero?
What exactly counts as 'far away' (how big must r be compared to a)?
teacher_script.board_action: Write on board header: Entry ticket answers: 1/r^2 or 1/r^3? Note common answers.
teacher_script.heading: Collect tickets & quick share
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Put your paper face-up on the desk so I can see your answer. I'll call on a few students. If you circled 1/r^2, be ready to say one sentence why; if you circled 1/r^3, be ready to explain what 'dipole moment' might mean." Walk to three students, read one answer aloud and ask: "Which of you wrote the opposite? Tell us your one-sentence reason." Keep the tone neutral. If a student says 'they cancel so field is zero', ask: "Is it zero for every r, or only in a special place?"

anticipated_questions: Why can we drop the higher order terms in a/r? How big is a/r allowed to be?
Where did the 4a come from in the numerator?
Why do we define p = q(2a) and not q a?
teacher_script.board_action: Write each step equations exactly as you derive: distances R± = r ∓ a; E = (1/4πϵ0) q[1/(r−a)^2 − 1/(r+a)^2]; show binomial expansion steps; final form proportional to p/(4πϵ0 r^3).
teacher_script.heading: Derive dipole far-field scaling (r >> a)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We'll derive how the field behaves far from a dipole made of +q at x=+a and −q at x=−a. Keep units: q in coulombs, distances in meters." Draw the two charges on the board. Step 1: Write Coulomb's law and point to each charge: use F formula as force and then convert to E by dividing by a test charge. Say: "Electric field of a point charge at distance R is E = (1/4πϵ0) q / R^2 in direction r̂." Step 2: For a point on the +x axis at coordinate x = r (r >> a), write distances to each charge: R+ = r−a, R− = r+a. Step 3: Write the fields from each: E+ = (1/4πϵ0) q/(r−a)^2 to the right; E− = (1/4πϵ0) (−q)/(r+a)^2 to the right (explain sign). Step 4: Add E = E+ + E−; show algebraic subtraction: factor (1/4πϵ0) q [1/(r−a)^2 − 1/(r+a)^2]. Step 5: Expand to leading order in a/r by using binomial approximation: 1/(r±a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2 (1 ∓ 2a/r + 3( a/r)^2 ...). Keep only first-order term in a/r after subtraction. Show result E ≈ (1/4πϵ0) * (q * 4a) / r^3. Then identify p = q(2a) and write E ∝ p / (4πϵ0 r^3). Emphasize units: p in C·m, E in N/C. Conclude: falls off as 1/r^3 for r >> a.

anticipated_questions: Our sensor readings are noisy — how do you know it's 1/r^3 and not experimental error?
What if I measure off the axis, does it still fall like 1/r^3?
Can we do this with bigger charges so it's clearer?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the measured sensor values and the ratios between distances; note comparison to 1/r^2 and 1/r^3 expected ratios.
teacher_script.heading: Short demo: measure idea of faster falloff
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "I'll show a quick demonstration with two small charged pith balls fixed at ±a and a small test probe on a rod. You will watch how the probe reading changes when I move it away." Place two opposite charges separated by known 2a (say a = 1 cm so 2a = 2 cm) and bring a small calibrated field sensor (or an electroscope with marked distances) along the axis; announce distances r = 5 cm, 10 cm, 20 cm. At each r, read sensor and say expected scaling: if 1/r^2 expected, ratio from 5→10 cm would be 1/4; if 1/r^3 expected ratio is 1/8. Ask students to watch which ratio matches experiment more closely. After readings, state observation: readings drop faster than 1/r^2 consistent with 1/r^3 scaling for r >> a.

anticipated_questions: Why are the end caps flux zero? Don't field lines hit them?
What does 'infinite line' mean practically — how long must it be?
Is Gauss's law always true even if field is not symmetric?
teacher_script.board_action: Write Gauss's law formula; draw cylinder with line charge; write flux = E(2π r L) = q_enc/ϵ0 and solve E = λ/(2πϵ0 r).
teacher_script.heading: Gauss's law quick review and line-charge example
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Quick Gauss's law reminder: the flux through a closed surface equals enclosed charge divided by ϵ0. Write the formula and then use a known example: infinite line charge." Point to the cylindrical Gaussian surface diagram. Ask: "What symmetry simplifies E on the curved side?" (Answer: radial and same magnitude). Walk through applying Gauss: flux through curved surface = E(2π r L) and flux through end caps = 0; enclosed q = λ L. Solve for E = λ/(2πϵ0 r). State units: λ in C/m, r in m, E in N/C. Emphasize this is a different falloff (1/r) from dipole and monopole cases and explain why symmetry and infinite extent change result.

anticipated_questions: Why do we multiply by e? Is charge always a multiple of e?
What about electrons (negative sign)? Should we put a minus?
How to estimate if n is very large like 10^9?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the worked conversion: q = n e = 20 × 1.60×10^-19 C = 3.2×10^-18 C. Note: e = 1.60×10^-19 C.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: numerical charge calculation q = n e
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now a short calculation: If a dust particle has net charge +20e, what is q in coulombs? Use e = 1.60×10^-19 C. Work with your partner and write the answer with units and an order-of-magnitude statement." Circulate for 2.5 minutes. After partners finish, call a student to write result: q = 20 × 1.60×10^-19 C = 3.2×10^-18 C. Ask: "What is an order-of-magnitude estimate?" (Answer: about 10^-18 C). Emphasize carrying units through.

anticipated_questions: For the quick check, why didn't you ask for the constant factor in the dipole field?
Will we need the exact prefactor p/(4πϵ0 r^3) later or just the 1/r^3 dependence?
Can we use Gauss's law to get the dipole field exactly?
teacher_script.board_action: Write final two quick-check questions and correct answers briefly.
teacher_script.heading: Quick check and consolidation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Two quick questions on your paper: (1) For a dipole with p = q(2a) = 4.0×10^-9 C·m, at r = 0.10 m along the axis, what is the expected scaling of the field with r (write only '1/r^2' or '1/r^3')? (2) Convert −5e to coulombs. Write answers and hand up." Wait 60–90 seconds, then read correct answers: (1) 1/r^3 (2) −8.0×10^-19 C. Finish: "Today we used Coulomb's law to get dipole far-field ~ p/(4πϵ0 r^3) and reviewed Gauss's law example for a line charge. Keep these results for next time when we draw field lines and compute torques."

bullet_points: Definition: E(r) is the vector field produced by charges; force on test charge q0 is F = q0 E(r). Units: N/C = V/m.
Field lines: tangent = field direction; density (lines per area ⟂ field) indicates relative strength; lines start on + and end on -; lines do not cross.
Flux through area element: dΦ = E · dS, where dS = n̂ dS (units: N·m^2/C). If E ⟂ area, dΦ = E dS; if at angle θ, dΦ = E dS cosθ.
Charge densities (macroscopic): σ = dQ / dS (C/m^2); λ = dQ / dl (C/m); ρ = dQ / dV (C/m^3).
Dipole torque (uniform E): τ = p × E. Uniform E → torque only (no net force). Non-uniform E → possible net force.
Common corrections: Number of drawn field lines is arbitrary; the physics is in field strength and line density. Neutral object can be attracted by induced polarization without net charge transfer.
diagrams_to_draw: Positive point charge with radial arrows; same picture next to it with twice as many arrows and note 'same field, drawing choice'.
Small rectangular area element with normal n̂ labeled, show angle θ between E and n̂, label dS and draw E vector. Annotate dΦ = E · dS.
Dipole: -q at x=-a, +q at x=+a, arrow p from -q to +q. Show uniform E vector and curved arrow indicating torque.
Sketch of charged rod (comb) near neutral paper bits showing induced polarization (charges separated in the paper) and attraction.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Use F = (1/4πε0) q1 q2 / r^2. r = 0.08 m. Compute numeric value: k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2, so F = 8.99×10^9*(4.0×10^-6 C)*(1.0×10^-6 C)/(0.08 m)^2 = 8.99×10^9*4.0×10^-12/0.0064 ≈ 5.61 N. Direction: both charges are positive so q1 repels q2; q2 is pushed in +x direction (away from q1). Answer must state 5.6 N, +x direction (or 'to the right').
checkpoint_questions.question: Two point charges q1 = +4.0 μC at x = 0 and q2 = +1.0 μC at x = 0.08 m lie on the x-axis. Using Coulomb's law, find the magnitude and direction of the force on q2 from q1. Show units.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Superposition: E_net = E_from(+2μC at 0) + E_from(+2μC at 0.20m). At x = 0.10 m the left +2μC (at 0) produces a field pointing to the right (away from positive), magnitude k*2μC/(0.10 m)^2. The right +2μC (at 0.20 m) produces a field pointing to the left, magnitude k*2μC/(0.10 m)^2. The magnitudes are equal, so the two contributions cancel and E_net ≈ 0 at x = 0.10 m. (A correct answer states directions of each contribution and concludes near zero net field.)
checkpoint_questions.question: Three point charges lie on the x-axis: +2 μC at x = 0, −1 μC at x = 0.10 m, and +2 μC at x = 0.20 m. Without heavy arithmetic, explain how you would use superposition to find the electric field at x = 0.10 m (the location of the −1 μC). State the direction of each contribution and whether the net field at that point is likely to point left or right.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Torque τ = p × E. With p = (3.0×10^-6 C·m) i-hat and E = (2.0×10^4 N/C) j-hat, τ = pE (i × j) = (3.0×10^-6)(2.0×10^4) k-hat = 6.0×10^-2 N·m k-hat (out of the page). State units N·m and direction ( +k or 'out of page'). Net force in a uniform field is zero because the forces on the positive and negative charges of the dipole are equal and opposite; only a torque remains.
checkpoint_questions.question: A permanent electric dipole with dipole moment p = 3.0×10^-6 C·m is placed in a uniform electric field E = (2.0×10^4 N/C) j-hat (i.e., upward). What is the torque on the dipole if p points along +i-hat (to the right)? Is there a net force on the dipole in this uniform field? Explain briefly.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Students draw radial arrows away from the + charge. For the paper+comb, many will write 'paper is attracted and becomes charged' or 'paper gets pulled (maybe charged)'. Correct responses to look for: radial field arrows for the + charge; for the paper, the correct explanation is 'paper is polarized (induced dipole) and is attracted without gaining net charge.'
entry_ticket.prompt: On the desk paper, draw quickly (1) a positive point charge and (2) a neutral small piece of paper near a charged comb. For each drawing, next to it write: 'Field direction near the charge?' and 'Does the paper become net charged or just pulled?'. Spend 3 minutes.

exit_ticket.prompt: Complete all three parts. (a) Two point charges are on the x-axis: q1 = +3.0 μC at x = 0.00 m and q2 = +3.0 μC at x = 0.10 m. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the electrostatic force on q2 from q1. Show units. (b) A uniform electric field E = 5.0×10^3 N/C points in the +x direction. A dipole with moment p = 2.0×10^-6 C·m is placed so p points along +x. Calculate the torque (magnitude and axis/direction) on the dipole and state whether a net force acts on it in that uniform field. (c) Now add a third charge q3 = +3.0 μC at x = 0.20 m. Using superposition, determine the net electric field at x = 0.05 m (midpoint between q1 and q2). Give magnitude, direction, and units.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student supplies: (a) numeric F from Coulomb's law with units and direction (about 10 N magnitude, +x direction) computed with k and r = 0.10 m; (b) torque τ = p×E with numeric value 1.0×10^-2 N·m (or equivalent) and direction (k-hat or 'out of page'), and an explicit statement that net force = 0 in a uniform field; (c) net E at x=0.05 m found by adding fields from q1 and q2 (and q3 if it contributes) with numeric magnitude, correct sign/direction along x, and units N/C. Answers must show the use of Coulomb/field formulas and indicate directions.

homework.submission_format: Show handwritten work photographed or neatly typed calculations; include numeric answers with units and brief explanations for the sketch and the qualitative dipole answer.
tasks: Problem 1 (15 min): Two charges qA = +5.0 μC at x = 0 and qB = −2.0 μC at x = 0.12 m. (a) Compute the force on qB due to qA (magnitude and direction). (b) Compute the electric field at x = 0.06 m (midway) by superposition; give value and direction in N/C. Show all steps with units.

Problem 2 (15 min): A dipole with moment p = 4.0×10^-6 C·m lies at the origin with its axis making 30° above the +x axis in a uniform field E = 4.0×10^3 N/C directed along +x. (a) Calculate the torque vector (magnitude and direction). (b) Suppose instead the dipole sits near a single positive point charge (non-uniform field). In 2–3 sentences, explain whether the dipole can experience a net force and why (no calculation required).

Sketching (10 min): Draw field-line diagrams (label directions and explain line-density meaning) for: (i) an isolated positive point charge, (ii) an electric dipole. Under each sketch write one sentence correcting the misconception that 'more drawn lines always means stronger field.'

mentor_moment.story: In a demo, a teacher combed hair, brought the charged comb near small bits of paper, and a student announced, 'the paper got charged.' The teacher asked how the paper could be attracted without net charge and used a free piece of paper to show one side pulled closer than the other.
mentor_moment.takeaway: A neutral object can be attracted by induction: the external field shifts charges inside the object, creating a dipole that feels a net attraction in a non-uniform field.
mentor_moment.title: Comb, paper, and the dipole idea

anticipated_questions: Student: So the paper never gets any extra charge? — Answer: It stays net neutral unless charge is actually transferred. The field separates charges inside it.
Student: But why do diagrams sometimes show many lines? — Answer: The number drawn is a choice; we use density of lines per area to indicate relative strength, not the absolute count.
teacher_script.board_action: Write two tiny student sketches pinned to the board: (1) a + with radial arrows; (2) a comb near paper with a note 'answers varied'. Underline the words 'induced dipole' and 'field direction vs. drawn lines'.
teacher_script.heading: Collect quick ideas; correct visible misconceptions
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Look at three students' quick drawings. Say: "Thanks — two quick checks. First drawing: point charge. Who drew field arrows? Hold up your paper. These arrows point away from a positive charge — good. Second: paper and comb — show one. I see answers saying 'paper becomes charged' and others saying 'paper is pulled.' Both are common. We'll clarify this now: neutral objects can be attracted without gaining net charge because the external field shifts charges inside the object and creates an induced dipole. I'll show a short demo in a moment." Pause to let students nod. Ask: "Why are radial arrows drawn? What do arrows show — direction or strength?" If students say direction, affirm; if someone says number of arrows, ask "Would drawing twice as many arrows change the real field?" and wait for responses to surface the count misconception.

anticipated_questions: Student: Why N/C equals V/m? — Answer: Give quick statement: 1 N/C is the force per unit charge, and a volt per meter is the potential change per distance; they are equivalent units for E here.
Student: Why use r-hat? — Answer: To emphasize E is a vector; r-hat gives direction (away from +, toward -).
teacher_script.board_action: Write the point-charge formula (see formulae). Below it, write the numeric example: k = 8.99e9 N·m^2/C^2; Q = 2.0e-6 C; r = 0.50 m; compute E = k Q / r^2 with units, and the numerical result.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce electric field and point-charge formula
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We define the electric field E as a vector field produced by a charge that tells us the force per unit test charge at each point. Physically, if a small test charge q0 is placed at r, the force is F = q0 E(r)." Point to a coordinate origin on the board. Continue: "For a point charge Q at the origin the field at position r is this vector (I will write it and then explain each part)." Write the formula shown below. Then read aloud each symbol: "1/(4 pi epsilon_0) is a constant with units N·m^2/C^2; Q is charge in coulombs C; r-hat is the unit vector pointing from the charge to the field point; r is the distance in meters. This gives E in units N/C (which is the same as V/m)." Ask: "If Q is positive, which way does r-hat point and which way does E point?" Wait for answer (away). Then do a quick numeric anchor: "If Q = +2.0 µC and a point is 0.50 m away, we can compute the magnitude: plug numbers: k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2, Q = 2.0×10^-6 C, r = 0.50 m. Calculate magnitude on the board and show units. (Do the arithmetic step-by-step.)"

anticipated_questions: Student: If I draw more lines will the flux change? — Answer: No — drawing more lines is only a drawing choice; flux is calculated from E and dS values.
Student: What if the field varies across the patch? — Answer: Then break into smaller patches and integrate (we'll do integrals next periods).
teacher_script.board_action: Draw: two versions of field-line diagrams around + (few lines and many lines) with an arrow 'density, not absolute count'. Draw a small rectangular patch, show n-hat, label dS, write dPhi = E · dS and note dS = n-hat dS and units.
teacher_script.heading: Field lines, density, and flux with small-area element
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now field lines are a helpful picture. Remember: a field line's tangent gives the local field direction. Density of lines per area perpendicular to the field shows relative strength — not the raw count of lines we draw." Draw on board: a positive charge with a few lines; then show the same with twice the drawn lines and explain both are valid; only density matters. Next: introduce flux. Draw a small flat patch with normal n-hat and label its area dS. Say: "Flux through this element is dPhi = E · dS. Here dS is the vector n-hat times the area magnitude (units m^2). If E is perpendicular and uniform over the patch, dPhi = E dS. If at an angle, it's E dS cos theta." Ask: "Why would flux be useful?" Accept answers like 'counts how much field passes through surface' and link to Gauss's law students saw before.

anticipated_questions: Student: Why doesn't the dipole get pushed along in a uniform field? — Answer: Because the forces on +q and -q are equal and opposite in a uniform field; they make a torque but sum to zero.
Student: How big is p? — Answer: p = q * separation vector (we won't derive units now, but p has units C·m).
teacher_script.board_action: Draw charged rod and paper bits photo/sketch; draw dipole +q and -q on x-axis and arrow p from -q to +q; write tau = p × E and note 'uniform E -> torque only, no net force; non-uniform E -> possible net force'.
teacher_script.heading: Demo: charged rod, paper bits, and induced dipole; torque on a dipole
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Perform demo: bring a charged PVC rod or comb and small bits of paper. Show attraction of paper bits. Say: "Watch orientation of bits as they approach: they align such that nearest charges attract. This shows induced polarization, not net charging." Next, draw a simple dipole: +q at x = +a and -q at x = -a. Label dipole moment p pointing from negative to positive. Say: "In a uniform field E a dipole feels a torque that tries to align p with E, but no net force because forces on +q and -q cancel. The torque is tau = p × E. I'll write that formula exactly as given." Write the torque formula and explain cross product direction using right-hand rule physically: "If p is to the right and E upward, torque points out of the board — that means it will rotate the dipole." Then ask: "Would a dipole in a non-uniform field have a net force?" Guide: "Yes, because the magnitudes on the two charges differ with position, producing a net force."

anticipated_questions: Student: For problem A, do we use superposition? — Answer: Yes, add fields from each point charge as vectors.
Student: For torque, why use sinθ? — Answer: Because tau = |p||E|sinθ for magnitude from cross product; if p is perpendicular to E, sinθ = 1.
teacher_script.board_action: Project the two problems, then after student work, write final answers with units: (A) E_net = compute and direction (show vector signs), (B) |tau| = p E sinθ with numbers and result; note 'no net force in uniform field'.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice and check for goals
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out a short worksheet (or project it) with two quick problems: (A) Three point charges: q1 = +2.0 µC at x=0, q2 = -1.0 µC at x=0.30 m. Find E at x = 0.15 m (midpoint) and state direction. (B) A dipole with p = 6.0×10^-9 C·m in a uniform E = 5.0×10^3 N/C upward. Find torque magnitude and will it translate? Give 5 minutes for students to work in pairs. Circulate and prompt: "Remember vector addition for fields, and use tau = pE sinθ for magnitude". After 4 minutes, collect one answer from the class and correct any common arithmetic errors.

bullet_points: Objectives: derive E for infinite line (λ), infinite plane (σ), thin spherical shell (q); set up integrals for continuous charge.
Infinite line: choose cylindrical Gaussian surface coaxial with wire; field radial and constant on curved surface.
Infinite plane: choose pillbox straddling the plane; field perpendicular and equal on both faces.
Spherical shell: choose spherical Gaussian surfaces; outside behaves like point charge, inside E = 0.
Integration idea: write dQ for element, apply Coulomb's law, integrate; symmetry simplifies integrals.
diagrams_to_draw: Long vertical charged wire with coaxial cylinder (radius r, length L). Label λ, r, L.
Infinite plane with a small pillbox crossing it (area A, half-height h).
Spherical shell radius R with Gaussian spheres r<R and r>R.
Small line element dl on wire with point at distance r and angle θ (for integral setup).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Apply Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε0. Only the curved cylindrical surface contributes because end caps are parallel to the field. Curved surface area = 2πrL, enclosed charge Q_enc = λL. So E(2πrL) = λL/ε0 → E(r) = λ/(2π ε0 r) directed radially outward. Units: N/C (or V/m).
checkpoint_questions.question: You choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L around an infinitely long line of charge with linear density λ. Write the integral form of Gauss's law for this surface, identify the surfaces that contribute, and solve for E(r).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Take a segment dx at position x along the line. dE from Coulomb's law: dE = (1/(4π ε0)) (λ dx)/(r^2 + x^2). The component along the line is dE_parallel = dE · cosθ with cosθ = x/√(r^2+x^2). For a symmetric element at +x and -x these parallel components cancel, so only radial component dE_radial = dE · (r/√(r^2+x^2)) remains. Use dE_radial = (1/(4π ε0)) (λ dx) r/(r^2+x^2)^(3/2) to integrate over x from -∞ to +∞.
checkpoint_questions.question: Write the integral expression for the electric field at a point a distance r from a short segment dx of an infinite line charge (linear density λ). Show one step that justifies why components along the line cancel, leaving only the radial component to integrate.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: By symmetry and Gauss's law: choose a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r<R centered on the shell. The enclosed charge is zero because all charge sits on the shell at radius R. Gauss's law gives ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε0 = 0, and by symmetry E is the same at every point on that sphere, so E = 0 inside. Units: N/C.
checkpoint_questions.question: For a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius R and total charge Q, explain qualitatively why the electric field is zero everywhere inside the shell (r < R) without doing any integrals.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Correct choice: B) E ∝ 1/r. Common incorrect answer: many students pick A) 1/r^2 because they generalize from point charges. The one-sentence explanation should say whether they thought the wire behaves like a point (1/r^2) or that symmetry of a line changes the geometric spreading to 1/r.
entry_ticket.prompt:
You have a very long, uniformly charged straight wire. Without calculation, which of these describes how the electric field magnitude E changes with distance r from the wire?
A) E ∝ 1/r^2  B) E ∝ 1/r  C) E = constant  D) E ∝ r
Circle one and write one short sentence explaining your choice (no calculation).

exit_ticket.prompt: An infinite plane sheet carries uniform surface charge density σ = 4.0 × 10^-6 C/m^2. Using Gauss's law, find the magnitude and direction of the electric field 3.0 cm on one side of the sheet. Show the Gaussian surface you choose and one sentence that justifies why E is constant on the chosen surface.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student draws a small pillbox crossing the plane, states flux equation E(2A) = σA/ε0, solves to get E = σ/(2ε0) = (4.0×10^-6)/(2ε0) ≈ 2.26×10^3 N/C and states field is normal to the plane away from the sheet (units N/C). They justify constancy by symmetry: the infinite plane is translationally invariant, so E is the same on each flat face.

homework.submission_format: One-page PDF with step-by-step solutions and final numeric answers; include units on every result.
tasks: Derive the electric field magnitude for an infinitely long line of charge by (a) setting up and evaluating the integral of Coulomb's law for a straight infinite line, and (b) re-deriving the same result using Gauss's law. Write both derivations step by step and show units. (~Hint: both should give E = λ/(2π ε0 r)).
Use Gauss's law to show the field of an infinite uniformly charged plane is E = σ/(2ε0). Draw the pillbox Gaussian surface, compute flux, and explain why the two faces contribute equally.

A thin spherical shell of radius R = 0.50 m carries total charge Q = 2.0 μC. (a) Calculate the magnitude and direction of the field at r = 0.30 m and at r = 1.0 m. (b) Briefly explain your result in one sentence each (why zero or why like a point charge).

mentor_moment.story: A student once integrated the line charge correctly but forgot to argue why axial components cancel, then kept an extra factor of 2 and got a wrong answer on the exam.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Always state the symmetry that makes components cancel before you integrate; it guides the setup and prevents algebraic mistakes.
mentor_moment.title: Watch the symmetry, not the algebra

anticipated_questions: Why must the wire be infinite? (To justify translational symmetry and ignore end effects.)
Is epsilon_0 the same as in Coulomb's law? (Yes; it's the permittivity of free space.)
What does 'thin spherical shell' mean? (Charge confined to radius R, zero thickness.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write objectives on the board (short). Underline 'line, plane, shell'.
teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets and announce goals
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Collect the tickets. Say: "Today we will derive the electric fields for three classic symmetric distributions: an infinite line of charge, an infinite plane sheet, and a thin spherical shell. By the end you should be able to derive each field using Gauss's law and set up an integral for a continuous distribution. Keep your entry ticket answer in mind — we will check it." Pause while collecting, then read one typical wrong answer aloud: "Some of you wrote 1/r^2 because you remembered the point-charge field — we'll see why a line is different."

anticipated_questions: Why ignore the flat ends of the cylinder? (Field is parallel to ends; no flux there by symmetry.)
What if the wire weren't infinite? (You would have end effects; symmetry fails.)
What is â_n? (The outward radial unit vector.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw wire and coaxial cylinder. Write: Q_enc = λ L. Write flux = E(2π r L). Write Gauss's law and algebra to E = λ/(2π ε0 r) â_n.
teacher_script.heading: Derive field of an infinite line charge using Gauss's law
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Draw a long vertical line on the board and put a small segment labeled 'lambda' (λ = linear charge density, C/m). Say: "We choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface coaxial with the wire. By symmetry the field points radially outward and has the same magnitude at every point on the curved side." Draw a cylinder of radius r and length L around the wire. Ask: "Which parts of the Gaussian surface contribute flux?" Wait for answers: the curved surface only. Then write Gauss's law: \Phi = Q_enc/ε0. Compute Q_enc = λ L. Compute flux = E(r) × (curved area) = E × (2π r L). Rearrange to solve for E: E = λ/(2π ε0 r). Say: "Direction: radial (n-hat)." Point to the entry-ticket misconception: "Notice this gives 1/r, not 1/r^2 — because the area of the curved surface grows like r, not r^2."

anticipated_questions: Why are there two E A terms for the plane? (Because flux passes through both faces of the pillbox with equal magnitude.)
For the shell, how can field outside be like a point charge? (Because symmetry and Gauss's law show only total charge matters for r>R.)
Does the plane result depend on r? (No — field is independent of distance for an infinite plane because flux through faces doesn't change with r.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw plane with pillbox and label A, h. Write Q_enc = σ A. Write 2 E A = σ A/ε0 -> E = σ/(2 ε0). Draw sphere with R and inner and outer Gaussian surfaces. Write outer: E(4π r^2)=q/ε0 -> E = q/(4π ε0 r^2). Write inside: Q_enc = 0 -> E = 0.
teacher_script.heading: Derive field of an infinite plane and thin spherical shell (Gauss's law)
teacher_script.speaker_notes:
First the infinite plane: Draw a large flat sheet and a small Gaussian pillbox that straddles the sheet (height 2h, faces area A). Say: "By symmetry field is perpendicular to the plane and has the same magnitude on both faces. The sides contribute no flux because field is parallel there." Write Q_enc = σ A (σ = C/m^2). Flux = E A + E A = 2 E A. Use Gauss's law: 2 E A = Q_enc/ε0 = σ A/ε0. Solve: E = σ/(2 ε0), direction normal to plane (two directions away from sheet).
Now the thin spherical shell: Draw a sphere of radius R with total charge q on the shell. Explain two regions:
- For r > R choose a spherical Gaussian surface radius r. Symmetry => E radial and constant. Q_enc = q. Flux = E (4π r^2). Gauss: E(4π r^2) = q/ε0 -> E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) r̂.
- For r < R choose a Gaussian sphere inside the shell. Q_enc = 0 because all charge sits at radius R. So flux = 0 => E = 0 inside.
Emphasize units at each step: λ (C/m), σ (C/m^2), q (C), ε0 (C^2/(N·m^2)).

anticipated_questions: Why not do the full integral now? (Time; Gauss is quicker for symmetric cases but integration is always possible.)
What cancels in the integral? (Axial components from elements above and below cancel by symmetry; radial components add.)
When must we use integration? (When symmetry is insufficient for Gauss's law.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write dQ = λ dl. Write dE = (1/(4π ε0)) dQ / s^2. Write integral form for E_r with a note 'symmetry reduces to previous expression'.
teacher_script.heading: Quick demonstration of integration idea (superposition)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Gauss's law used symmetry. The same answers can be reached by integrating Coulomb's law. I'll set up the integral briefly for the line to show the idea." Draw a small line element dl at coordinate along the wire and a point at radial distance r. Write dQ = λ dl. Write Coulomb's law contribution magnitude dE = (1/(4π ε0)) dQ / (distance^2) times cosine factor. Show that integrating around the full infinite wire, the axial components cancel and the radial components add to give E ∝ 1/r. Do not carry out the full integral (time), but write the integral setup: E_r = ∫ (1/4π ε0) (λ dl cosθ)/s^2 and note symmetry/geometry reduces it to previous result. Emphasize you can always set up such integrals for less symmetric cases.

anticipated_questions: What if the plane is finite — does E stay constant? (No; edge effects make E vary with distance.)
How large should L be when using the cylinder? (Large compared to r; 'infinite' is an idealization.)
Can I always pick any Gaussian surface? (Yes, but pick one that matches symmetry so E is constant on parts of the surface.)
teacher_script.board_action: Box the three final formulae and write units beside each: λ (C/m), σ (C/m^2), q (C); write ε0 units C^2/(N·m^2).
teacher_script.heading: Check understanding and consolidate
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask three quick cold-call questions, one per result: (1) "For an infinite line, how does E change with r?" (expect '1/r' and point to formula). (2) "For an infinite plane sheet, what is E and why does it not depend on r?" (expect 'σ/(2ε0)', argue from pillbox). (3) "Inside a thin spherical shell is E zero — why?" (expect 'Q_enc = 0 inside, so by Gauss E=0'). Write: "If time, copy the boxed formulae and label units." Walk the room while students copy. Collect any final questions and answer briefly.

applications.context: Everyday electrostatics demonstration (charged comb and neutral paper).
applications.description: Explaining why a comb attracts small pieces of paper after combing dry hair.

evidence.quote: Taking the clue from the preceding discussion, the charged comb ‘polarises’ the piece of paper, i.e., induces a net dipole moment in the direction of field. Further, the electric field due to the comb is not uniform. This non-uniformity of the field makes a dipole to experience a net force on it.

applications.context: Design and analysis of spherically symmetric charged bodies and shielding approximations.
applications.description: Use of Gauss's law to justify that the electric field outside a uniformly charged spherical shell is the same as if charge were concentrated at the centre (application to shielding and spherical conductors).

evidence.quote: Thus for points outside the shell, the field due to a uniformly charged shell is as if the entire charge of the shell is concentrated at its centre.

Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from
static charges .

concepts.name: Electrostatics
concepts.summary: Study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges.

evidence.quote: like charges repel and unlike charges attract each other.
By convention, the charge on glass rod or cat’s fur is called positive and that on plastic rod or silk is termed negative.

concepts.name: Electric charge
concepts.summary: An attribute of matter responsible for electric interactions; comes in two polarities and can be transferred between bodies by rubbing.

evidence.quote: Experimentally it is established that all free charges are integral multiples e q of a basic unit of charge denoted by . Thus charge on a body is always given by q = ne where n is any integer, positive or negative.

concepts.name: Quantisation of charge
concepts.summary: Observable free charges occur in integer multiples of a basic unit e (magnitude of electron/proton charge).

evidence.quote: When some charge is transferred to a conductor, it readily gets distributed over the entire surface of the conductor. In contrast, if some charge is put on an insulator, it stays at the same place.

concepts.name: Conductors and insulators
concepts.summary: Materials classified by whether they allow electric charges (electrons) to move freely (conductors) or not (insulators); charges on conductors redistribute over the surface while on insulators they stay localized.

evidence.quote: Experimentally, it is verified that force on any charge due to a number of other charges is the vector sum of all the forces on that charge due to the other charges, taken one at a time.

Superposition Principle : The principle is based on the property that the
forces with which two charges attract or repel each other are not
affected by the presence of a third (or more) additional charge(s).

concepts.name: Principle of superposition
concepts.summary: Net electrostatic force on a charge from multiple other charges equals the vector sum of the forces due to each charge taken individually; individual pairwise forces are unaffected by presence of others.
